soundTherapy.title: Sound Therapy: Soothing Sounds and Frequencies
soundTherapy.description: Listen to frequencies and binaural beats to relax, ease anxiety and support your focus.

playingState.description: Let the sounds surround you. Focus on your breath and let the frequencies guide you into deep relaxation.
playingState.instructions: Close your eyes and allow the vibrations to penetrate deeply, bringing peace to your mind and body.

howItWorks.title: How Sound Therapy Works
howItWorks.description1: A soft, steady sound gives your attention something to rest on: as you listen, you step back a little from thoughts that go round in circles. With headphones, binaural beats play two slightly different tones in each ear; the brain then perceives a slow pulse that many people find soothing.
howItWorks.description2: Effects vary from person to person: there is no 'right' frequency. What matters is choosing a sound you find pleasant, at a moderate volume, and pairing it with calm breathing.
howItWorks.description3: Used regularly, listening can become a relaxation ritual, for example before sleep or after a busy day. Research on sounds and binaural beats is still limited: sound therapy complements other techniques and does not replace professional support.

brainwaveEntrainment.title: An anchor for your attention
brainwaveEntrainment.description: Focusing on a sound helps slow the flow of thoughts and bring you back to the present moment.

autonomicBalance.title: A rhythm that invites calm
autonomicBalance.description: Combined with slow breathing, listening can help the body relax and the heart slow down.

physiologicalResonance.title: A moment for yourself
physiologicalResonance.description: Taking a few minutes to listen with your eyes closed is already giving yourself a break.

science.title: What Studies Say
science.description: Listening to calming music has been studied for anxiety, mostly in hospital patients. Binaural beats have been studied much less, and specific 'frequencies' not seriously at all.
science.bottomLine: listening to sounds or music you find soothing can help you relax. Research remains limited: it is a complement, not a treatment.

music.title: Music for people with cancer
music.what: Listening to recorded music for 15 to 60 minutes, compared with usual care.
music.result: Patients who listened to music were less anxious (medium effect).
music.caution: Results varied widely between trials; few high-quality trials.

binaural.title: Binaural beats
binaural.who: Participants in 22 studies, mostly in laboratory settings.
binaural.what: The effect of binaural beats on memory, attention, anxiety and pain.
binaural.result: A medium effect overall, which depends heavily on the frequency used and listening time.
binaural.caution: Results for anxiety are not reported separately, and the studies differ widely.

whenToPractice.title: When to Practice
items: When feeling overwhelmed, anxious, or unable to settle your mind
Before a medical procedure, a stressful event or an important conversation, to settle yourself
When anxiety rises, to give yourself a pause and support your breathing
At bedtime, to unwind and prepare for sleep

whatYoullNotice.title: What You Might Notice
items: A sense of relaxation settling in after a few minutes of listening
Breathing that slows down and muscles that loosen
A little more distance from thoughts that go round in circles
With regular practice, a relaxation ritual that is easier to return to

headphones.title: Headphones
headphones.description: Use stereo headphones for binaural beats to work properly. Each ear must hear a distinct frequency.

environment.title: Environment
environment.description: Find a quiet, comfortable space where you won't be interrupted. Dim lighting or closed eyes enhance focus on the sounds.

consistency.title: Consistency
consistency.description: A few minutes a day is enough: regular practice helps make listening a go-to way to relax.
